overview.text: Graphene is a form of carbon consisting of a single atomic layer in a repeating hexagonal, honeycomb-like arrangement. It is the basic building sheet of graphite: stacked layers make the material used in pencil cores. Unlike ordinary graphite, an isolated graphene sheet is only one atom thick, yet it is flexible and conducts heat and electricity exceptionally well. Isolating and studying individual sheets helped establish research into two-dimensional materials. Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov isolated graphene at the University of Manchester in 2004 by peeling layers from graphite with adhesive tape; their experiments on graphene received the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.

key_facts.text: Graphene is one layer of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb lattice.
It is a building block of graphite, the material used in pencil cores.
Geim and Novoselov isolated graphene at Manchester in 2004 using adhesive tape to peel layers from graphite.
Graphene is flexible and conducts heat and electricity exceptionally well despite being one atom thick.
The researchers’ graphene experiments were recognized with the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.
